parts.note: B is the standard abbreviation for British
someone clean-shaven has no facial hair, i.e. lacks a beard

explanation.surface: A question about whether a pirate from Britain ought to shave off his whiskers.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the most famous bearded pirate is built from the very idea of having no beard.
explanation.definitionFit: Blackbeard was the nickname of Edward Teach, a notorious early eighteenth-century pirate captain.

clue.text: Get on in the sack — produce baby?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to mate, as animals do
second meaning: to bring forth offspring

explanation.surface: A cheeky question about whether getting along in bed leads to a pregnancy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get on in the sack' sounds like getting along well in bed, which here simply means mating.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both the act of mating and the resulting reproduction of young.

clue.text: When one may legally agree to scene of nag being shot

indicators.note: something shot is wrecked or ruined, so the letters are knocked out of their order

parts.note: all twelve letters used as fodder

explanation.surface: Someone consents to visit the place where an old horse is being put down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' looks like a link word but its letters are needed in the fodder; a nag is a worn-out horse.
explanation.definitionFit: The age of consent is the legal minimum age at which a person can agree to sexual activity.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: thoughtful and generous towards others
second meaning: a type or category

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it describes a thoughtful person; apart, an adjective and a noun meaning type.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an adjective for gentle helpfulness and a noun for a class or variety.

parts.note: surface reading: to team up or combine efforts with someone
setter's reading: to sign up to the armed forces

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for collaborating is read literally: joining the forces means becoming a soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: To sign up for military service is to become a member of the army, navy or air force.

indicators.note: a thing that blocks a way sits inside it, so one piece goes in the middle of the other

parts.note: a route is a path or way
let means permitted

explanation.surface: A sport is permitted to obstruct a footpath.
explanation.definitionFit: Roulette is a casino gambling game played with a spinning wheel and a ball.

clue.text: Chain of events with disastrous end: come off it

indicators.note: a disastrous outcome leaves things in a mess, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sequence of happenings ending in catastrophe, greeted with an exasperated 'come off it'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disastrous end' reads as a single phrase in the surface, but only 'end' is fodder and 'disastrous' scrambles it along with 'come off it'.
explanation.definitionFit: The domino effect is a cumulative sequence where one event triggers the next, like toppling dominoes in a line.

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
to bear a load is to take it

explanation.surface: Little bears are competing in a horse race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bears' looks like a plural noun for the animals but is a verb meaning endures or takes.
explanation.definitionFit: Stakes is used in race names such as the Diamond Stakes, a horse race with prize money put up by owners.

indicators.note: to enter something is to go inside it, so one piece sits within the other
something wild is unruly and out of order, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: a lea is a meadow; its letters are rearranged and split around the bird
a tern is a common seabird

explanation.surface: An immortal seabird swoops down into an untamed meadow.
explanation.definitionFit: Something deathless never dies, which is to say it lasts for ever without end.

indicators.note: a thing that disintegrates falls to pieces, so the letters are reassembled differently

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A boat going down is on the point of breaking up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sinking vessel' suggests a ship going down, but here it means a vessel that sinks other ships, a German submarine.
explanation.definitionFit: A U-boat was a German submarine, notorious for torpedoing and sending Allied ships to the bottom.

indicators.note: discarded means thrown away, so that letter is removed

parts.note: a draft is a preliminary sketch

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the word just before it

parts.note: the first letter of the painter's name

explanation.surface: A silly drawing that the Dutch master threw out at the start.
explanation.definitionFit: Daft is a mainly British informal word for foolish or stupid.

clue.text: One among the stars in M*A*S*H

definitions.text: One among the stars in M*A*S*H

parts.words: One among the stars in M*A*S*H
parts.note: surface reading: a cast member of the TV series M*A*S*H

parts.words: One among the stars in M*A*S*H
parts.note: setter's reading: one of the star-shaped symbols printed in the title

explanation.walkthrough: The stars are not actors but the little typographic symbols between the letters of the show's title.
explanation.definitionFit: The star-shaped printing symbol is used for footnotes and, here, decoratively in a title.

clue.text: Dodgy old boiler with no current in madam's house

indicators.note: something dodgy is unreliable or crooked, so the letters are rearranged
with no means lacking, so that symbol is taken out

parts.note: taken as written
I is the symbol for electric current in physics

explanation.surface: A faulty old boiler with no power in the house of a lady of the manor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'madam' looks like a polite title, but here it is the woman who runs a brothel.
explanation.definitionFit: A bordello is a brothel, an establishment run by a madam where prostitutes work.

clue.text: Post Office holding very popular image

indicators.note: something holding another clasps it inside, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: PO is the abbreviation for Post Office
a hot item is very much in demand

explanation.surface: The Post Office has an image that is in great demand.
explanation.definitionFit: A photo, short for photograph, is a picture taken with a camera.

clue.text: Opening wine that goes with almost everything

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter is cut off

parts.note: port is a fortified Portuguese wine
all means everything

explanation.surface: A wine that pairs with nearly every dish is a good opening.
explanation.definitionFit: A portal is a doorway or gateway, an opening through which one enters.

indicators.note: a leader is at the front, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the party name
food that goes off rots

explanation.surface: The Conservative leader turns against left-wing activists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes off' reads as 'goes off on a rant at' but means decays; Trots is slang for Trotskyists.
explanation.definitionFit: Trots is an informal, often dismissive name for Trotskyists, followers of the revolutionary Leon Trotsky.

parts.note: surface reading: a bomb or blast going off beneath a river crossing
setter's reading: the bridge is that of the nose, beneath which a sudden involuntary burst of air comes out

explanation.walkthrough: The bridge is the bony ridge at the top of the nose, not a structure over a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A sneeze is a sudden violent expulsion of air through the nose and mouth.

clue.text: Hoover perhaps, but no power for householder

indicators.note: but no means except without, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: Herbert Hoover was a US president; 'perhaps' marks him as an example
P is the abbreviation for power in physics

explanation.surface: A vacuum cleaner that has no electricity is of little use to the person running a home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hoover' suggests the vacuum cleaner brand, but it is Herbert Hoover, US president 1929 to 1933.
explanation.definitionFit: A resident is someone who lives in a particular house, as a householder does.

clue.text: Ace, then service returned at a distance

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for ace on playing cards

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: the Royal Air Force is one of the armed services

explanation.surface: A tennis player serves an ace and then a return comes back from far away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ace' and 'service' paint a tennis scene, but service means an armed force, the RAF.
explanation.definitionFit: Afar is an adverb meaning far away or from a long way off.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: bad-tempered or tetchy, in informal British use

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the literal second sense: full of rats.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective is informal British slang for grumpy and also literally describes a place teeming with rodents.

parts.note: to have accomplished something is to have done it
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: The lover of the Trojan hero achieved nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Dido, queen of Carthage in Virgil's Aeneid, fell in love with Aeneas and killed herself when he left.

clue.text: Cancel yearbook with second article expunged

indicators.note: expunged means erased, and second points to which of the repeated letters goes

parts.note: an annual is a book published once a year
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A publisher scraps a yearbook after a second piece in it is struck out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'article' looks like a piece of writing in the yearbook, but it is the grammatical article A, and only the second A in the word is removed.
explanation.definitionFit: To annul is to declare void or invalid, as with a marriage or contract, i.e. to cancel it.

clue.text: Renowned inn — meet to get sloshed

indicators.note: getting sloshed means getting drunk, and drunken letters stagger out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A famous pub where people gather to get drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Eminent describes someone famous and respected within a particular sphere.

indicators.note: something new is made afresh, so the letters are formed into a different word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A planning idea about new towns is said to be remarkable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New town' reads as a planned British settlement, but 'New' is only the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Something noteworthy deserves attention because it is interesting or significant, hence remarkable.
